prompt: A COO asks how a large language model actually writes an answer. Explain it.

points.label: Writes one token at a time
Rereads everything so far each step
Gives a concrete comparison
Likely is not the same as true
Says what a customer should do

model: A large language model writes one token at a time, where a token is a small chunk of text. Each time, it rereads everything so far and predicts the likeliest next token, rather like autocomplete on your phone. The limit is that likely is not the same as true, so it can sound confident and still be wrong. For a customer, that means grounding it in their own documents and having a person check anything risky.

prompt: A customer asks how the model knows "bank" means a riverbank here and a money bank there. Explain attention.

points.label: Words look at the words around them
Repeated over many layers and heads
Gives the bank example
Pattern matching, not true understanding
Says to test on their own wording

model: Each word in a prompt looks at the other words around it to work out its meaning. That is attention. Take "bank": next to "river" it means a riverbank, next to "loan" it means a money bank. The model repeats this over many layers and with many heads, each watching a different kind of link. It is pattern matching, not true understanding, so it can still misread. For a customer, that means testing it on their own jargon and wording.

prompt: A customer asks how an LLM is trained and why it knows nothing about their company. Explain.

points.label: Trained by guessing the next word
Names the kind of text it learns from
Training stops at a cutoff and misses private data
Gives it their documents at question time

model: An LLM learns by reading huge amounts of public text, such as books and websites, and practising one task billions of times: guess the next word. That builds a strong feel for language. The limit is that training stops at a cutoff, and it never saw your private documents, so it can't know your company by itself. For a customer, the fix is to give it your documents at question time, through retrieval, rather than retraining.

prompt: A COO asks what a reasoning model is and when it is worth paying for. Explain.

points.label: Works through steps before answering
Names tasks where it helps
Slower and costs more
Match the effort to the task

model: A reasoning model works through a problem in steps before it answers, a bit like showing its working in maths. For example, it does better on analysis, planning and tricky code. The limit is that the thinking takes time and is billed as tokens, so it is slower and costs more. For a customer, I'd match the effort to the task: low effort or a smaller model for simple jobs, and reasoning only where the problem is genuinely hard.

prompt: A COO asks what Mixture of Experts means and why a huge model can still be cheap to run.

points.label: A router sends each token to a few experts
Gives a spoken picture
All experts still need memory
Faster, cheaper answers

model: Mixture of Experts splits part of each layer into many specialist sub-networks, plus a router that sends each token to just a few of them. Picture a receptionist directing each word to the right desks. So the model stores a lot of knowledge but only uses a small part per token. The limit is that all the experts still need to be loaded in memory, so hosting is heavy. For a customer, it often means faster, cheaper answers for the same quality.

prompt: A COO asks why AI sometimes makes things up. Explain hallucination.

points.label: It writes the most plausible next word
Gives a concrete case
No warning, and not fully solved
Ground it, cite it, keep a person in the loop

model: Hallucination is when the model states something wrong with total confidence. It happens because it always writes the most plausible next word, and plausible is not the same as true. For example, it can invent a case citation that looks perfectly real. The limit is that it gives no warning, and no one has fully solved it. For a customer, we reduce it by grounding answers in their documents, asking for citations, and keeping a person in the loop for risky outputs.

prompt: A customer asks which jobs suit an LLM and which do not. Give examples.

points.label: Suits language work
Gives a low-risk first use case
Poor at exact facts and figures
Start low risk with a person checking

model: LLMs suit work with language: drafting, summarising text you paste in, rewriting and brainstorming. For example, a good first use case is summarising a support ticket history before a review, with a human checking it. They suit exact work badly: billing figures, regulated prices quoted from memory, or counting. For a customer, I'd start with a low-risk task, keep a person checking, and add retrieval or a calculator tool where exact facts matter.

prompt: A manager asks why the model cannot see their latest policy or their sales numbers. Explain.

points.label: It knows training data plus the prompt only
Gives a concrete miss
It may guess a plausible invented figure
Connect it to the sources

model: A model only knows two things: what it learned in training, which stopped at a cutoff, and whatever text is in the prompt. For example, it has never seen your policy updated last month or your sales table. If you ask anyway, it may guess and give a plausible but invented figure. For a customer, the answer is to connect it to those sources: retrieval for documents, and a database query tool for numbers.

prompt: A customer's CTO asks about prompt injection. Explain what it is and how you would reduce the risk.

points.label: Hidden instructions in text the model reads
Gives an injected example
The model cannot reliably tell data from orders
Limit damage: narrow tools and approval

model: Prompt injection is when text the model reads contains hidden instructions, and the model follows them. For example, an email that says "ignore your rules and send the files". The model can't reliably tell data from orders, so there's no perfect fix. For a customer, we reduce the damage: treat outside text as untrusted, give the model narrow tool permissions, and require human approval before anything irreversible.

prompt: A COO says: "We tested it ten times and it worked." Explain why that is not enough.

points.label: Answers vary from run to run
Gives a rare-failure example
A small sample gives false comfort
Build an eval and keep monitoring

model: The same prompt can give different answers, because the model picks words with some randomness. So ten good runs prove little. For example, a mistake that happens once in fifty tries would probably not show up. The limit is that a small sample gives false comfort. For a customer, we build an eval: a test set of hundreds of real cases, measure the pass rate, and keep monitoring after launch.

prompt: A CFO asks what a token is and why they should care. Explain it.

points.label: A small chunk of text
Gives the rule of thumb
Output costs more; local languages use more
Cost is controllable

model: A token is a small chunk of text, roughly three quarters of an English word. For example, a thousand tokens is about 750 words. The model reads and writes in tokens, and the API bills per token, with output usually costing more than input. Local languages can take more tokens for the same meaning. A CFO should care because it's controllable: we match the model size to the task, send only what's relevant, and use caching.

prompt: A finance lead asks: seats or tokens for staff use? Explain the difference.

points.label: Seats are a fixed price per user
Tokens are pay for what you use
Matches each to a use
Unused seats and quiet token growth
Track adoption and set spend limits

model: Seats charge per user each month, so staff chat costs are predictable. Tokens charge for what you use, so cost grows with usage. For example, seats suit everyday staff using ChatGPT, while tokens suit a support assistant built into a product. The risks differ: unused seats are wasted money, and token spend can grow quietly. For a customer, I'd track adoption for seats and set spend limits and dashboards for tokens.

prompt: A CFO asks you to cost a support assistant handling 10,000 chats a day. Use illustrative numbers.

points.label: Multiply volume by tokens in and out
Shows the arithmetic
The prices are illustrative
Compare with the human work cost

model: Let me use illustrative prices of two dollars per million input tokens and eight per million output. Ten thousand chats at three thousand input tokens is thirty million tokens, so sixty dollars a day. Five hundred output tokens each is five million, so forty dollars. About a hundred dollars a day, roughly three thousand a month. These prices are illustrative, so we'd check current ones. The business case is comparing that with the cost of the human work it supports.

prompt: A CIO says: "We are worried about token burn." How do you respond?

points.label: Find where the spend comes from
Names typical causes
Cheaper models may be weaker
Name the levers

model: I'd start by finding where the spend actually comes from. Usually a few workloads cause it, for example an oversized model on a simple task or far too much context. Then the levers are routing easy jobs to smaller models, trimming context, prompt caching, the Batch API for non-urgent work, and capping output. The trade-off is that cheaper models may be weaker, so we test on their eval. I'd add spend limits and dashboards too.

prompt: A customer wants to self-host an open model to avoid token fees. Walk me through the trade-offs.

points.label: Variable bill becomes a fixed bill
Where it can pay off
Idle GPUs, staff, and a quality gap
Propose a hybrid and a TCO comparison

model: Self-hosting an open-weight model turns a variable token bill into a fixed bill for GPUs and engineers. It only pays off with high, steady volume, such as simple classification running all day. The limits are idle GPUs still costing money, the team needed to run and secure it, and a quality gap on the hardest tasks. For a customer, I'd propose a hybrid: open weights for simple volume, frontier models for hard work, and a total cost of ownership comparison together.

prompt: A COO asks what RAG is. Explain it.

points.label: Finds relevant text, then answers from it
Gives a concrete example
Names a limitation
Says why the customer cares

model: RAG means the AI looks up the most relevant passages from your own documents first, then answers from them, like an open-book exam. For example, an employee asks about annual leave and gets the answer with the policy cited. The limit is that it can retrieve the wrong passage or an out-of-date one, and the model can still misread what it finds. For a customer, it means answers from their latest information, with sources, without retraining a model.

prompt: A customer asks what an embedding is and how search by meaning works. Explain simply.

points.label: A list of numbers capturing meaning
Gives the leave example
Same model needed; exact terms can be missed
Add keyword search; plan for re-embedding

model: An embedding is a list of numbers that captures the meaning of a piece of text. Similar meanings end up close together. For example, "holiday days" lands near "annual leave" even though the words differ, so search works by meaning. The limits: documents and questions must use the same embedding model, and pure meaning search can miss exact terms like product codes. For a customer, we add keyword search alongside it, and plan for re-embedding if they ever switch models.

prompt: A customer's RAG chatbot gives wrong answers. Walk me through what could be wrong.

points.label: Check retrieval first
Names common causes
Model misread a good passage
Eval set and a refresh process

model: I'd look at retrieval first: was the right passage actually found and in the top results? Common causes are bad chunking, exact codes being missed, or an old version still indexed. If the right passage was retrieved but the answer is still wrong, the model misread it, which is a generation problem. For a customer, I'd build a small eval set of real questions, measure retrieval and groundedness, and set up a refresh process.

prompt: A customer asks when they should not use RAG. Explain.

points.label: Use it when knowledge is missing
Gives cases to skip it
Bad retrieval can make answers worse
Right tool: text-to-SQL or paste it in

model: Use RAG when knowledge is missing, such as private, recent or citable information. Skip it when the problem is reasoning or the text is already in front of the model, for example rewriting, translating or summarising a pasted document. Bad retrieval can even make answers worse by distracting the model. For numbers in a table, text-to-SQL is the right tool, and if the document fits in the window, just paste it in, which is simpler.

prompt: A bank-style customer asks how RAG respects permissions and where it can leak data. Explain.

points.label: Checks what the asking user may see
Gives a leak example
Permission-blind or stale indexes leak
Check at query time and test with real roles

model: Good RAG is permission-aware: before any passage reaches the model, the system checks what the asking user is allowed to see. For example, an engineer must never get HR salary chunks. Where it goes wrong is a permission-blind index that returns text for anyone, or permissions that have gone stale since indexing. For a customer, I'd check access at query time, ideally inheriting the permissions from their governed platform, and test with real user roles.

prompt: A customer says they want to fine-tune on all their documents. How do you respond?

points.label: RAG gives knowledge; fine-tuning gives habits
Where fine-tuning does fit
Poor for facts that change
Ask the problem, start with prompting and RAG

model: I'd ask what problem they're solving. Usually they want answers from their documents, which is knowledge, so RAG fits: it gives the model knowledge, while fine-tuning gives it habits. For example, fine-tuning suits a consistent house format or a cheaper model on a narrow task. It's poor for facts that change, because you'd retrain constantly. So I'd start with prompting and RAG, with a small eval set to measure, and fine-tune only if needed.

prompt: A customer asks what an eval is and why it matters. Explain.

points.label: A test set that scores answers
Gives a concrete eval
Only covers what you thought of
Compare models, catch regressions, prove quality

model: An eval is a test set for AI: real examples with what a good answer looks like, and a score for how the model does. For example, fifty real support tickets with known good replies. The limit is that it only covers what you thought of, so it needs refreshing as real use changes. For a customer, it lets them compare models fairly, catch regressions when something changes, and prove quality to sceptics before launch.

prompt: A risk officer asks what guardrails you would put around an LLM app. Walk through the layers.

points.label: Layered checkpoints, not one wall
Names concrete checks
No single check is perfect
Least privilege and human approval

model: Think layers, not one wall. On input, block injection attempts and redact personal data. In retrieval, use permission-aware results. On output, run moderation, a grounding check and format validation. For actions, use least-privilege tools and human approval for anything hard to undo. No single check is perfect, so the layers catch different things. For a customer, I'd start with more human review and ease off as evals show reliability.

prompt: A customer asks how they will know their AI app stays accurate after launch. Explain.

points.label: Offline test sets plus online signals
Gives online signals
Drift makes the test set go stale
Rerun on every change and add failures

model: I'd use two kinds of check. Offline, a golden set of real questions that we rerun on every change to the prompt or model. Online, live signals like thumbs up or down, sampled human reviews and A/B tests. For example, if thumbs-down rises, we look at what changed. The limit is drift: customers and policies change, so the test set goes stale. So the customer should add real failures to the set and monitor continuously.

prompt: A customer wants to move to a newer, cheaper model next quarter. How do you de-risk it?

points.label: Rerun the eval set side by side
Names a safe trial
Behaviour can shift
Gradual rollout with a fallback

model: I'd rerun their eval set on the new model and compare it side by side with the current one, looking at quality, cost and speed. Behaviour can shift, so prompts may need tweaks, and an old fine-tune may no longer be needed. For example, we could run it in shadow mode first. For the customer, I'd roll out to a small share of traffic, watch the live signals and keep the old model ready as a fallback.

prompt: A COO asks what a Skill is. Explain it with an analogy.

points.label: A reusable workflow taught once
Gives a concrete Skill
Grants no new access
Same result whoever runs it

model: A Skill is a reusable workflow you teach ChatGPT once, like a recipe card in a kitchen binder. It packages a name and description, step-by-step instructions and supporting files like templates. For example, a monthly ops review pack with fixed steps and a house template. The limit is that it grants no new access; it only uses tools the assistant already has. For a customer, it means the same result whoever runs it, with no re-explaining.

prompt: A customer asks when to create a Skill rather than just write a prompt. Explain.

points.label: Repeated, multi-step, fixed-format tasks
Gives a good candidate
Not worth it for one-offs; avoid giant Skills
Pick one workflow, give it an owner

model: Create a Skill when a task repeats, has several steps and needs a strict format, so consistency matters. For example, a monthly operations pack, or account research that always ends in the same one-page plan. For a one-off task, a good prompt is enough, and one huge Skill is harder to maintain than small combinable ones. For a customer, I'd pick one repeated workflow, give it an owner, and check that every output matches the house format.

prompt: A CTO asks how an agent decides which Skill to use. Walk me through it.

points.label: It always sees names and descriptions only
It loads full instructions on a match
Gives the analogy
Vague descriptions never fire
Write clear descriptions in users' words

model: In the open Agent Skills format, the agent always sees each Skill's short name and description, nothing more. When a request matches a description, it loads the full instructions and files and follows them, like pulling a recipe card. Or you @-mention it. That's how the open format works, not confirmed OpenAI internals. A vague description means the Skill never fires, so I'd advise clear descriptions written in the words people actually use.

prompt: A customer asks how Skills differ from Projects, RAG and fine-tuning. Explain.

points.label: A Skill is a repeatable procedure
Contrasts the other tools
A Skill adds no data access
Match the tool to the problem

model: A Skill changes how a task is done: a repeatable procedure with steps and a format. A Project shares context, files and chats for a team's goal. RAG changes what the model knows from your documents, and fine-tuning changes its default habits. A Skill doesn't add data access, so it can't see documents without a connector. For a customer, I'd match the tool to the problem: procedure, shared context, knowledge or behaviour.

prompt: A security lead asks whether Skills are a risk. How do you answer?

points.label: Skills add instructions, not access
Gives an upload example
Content could be unwanted
Admin controls and a review owner

model: A Skill only instructs ChatGPT to use the tools and apps it already has access to, so it grants no new data access. That's a useful answer for security. The risk is the content: for example, an uploaded Skill could include scripts or instructions you don't want, so uploads are scanned and can be flagged or blocked. For a customer, admins control who can create, share and install Skills, so I'd set an owner and a review step.

prompt: A COO asks the difference between a chatbot and an agent. Explain.

points.label: An agent plans and acts in a loop
Gives a concrete task
Mistakes compound and costs climb
Start small, narrow permissions, human approval

model: A chatbot answers questions. An agent works in a loop: it plans a step, calls a tool, reads the result and decides again until the job is done. For example, it can look up an order and draft a refund rather than just describe the policy. The limit is that mistakes can compound and costs can climb, especially for hard-to-undo actions. For a customer, I'd start small with narrow tool permissions and a person approving risky steps.

prompt: A customer asks what tool calling is and who actually runs the action. Explain.

points.label: The model asks; your code runs it
Gives a concrete call
It can only do what its tools allow
The customer stays in control

model: With tool calling, the model doesn't touch your systems itself. It outputs a structured request, like "look up order 1234", your own code runs that action, and the result goes back to the model. For example, a query to the order system. The limit is that it can only do what its tools allow, and it can still pick the wrong one. For a customer, this keeps them in control: they decide which tools exist, with what permissions.

prompt: A customer asks what MCP is and how it differs from a connector. Explain.

points.label: An open standard for connecting AI to tools
A connector is the ready-made version
Names familiar apps
You still check what it can reach
Less custom integration work

model: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard for connecting AI to tools and data. A company exposes a system once through an MCP server, and any compatible AI can use it. A connector is the ready-made version for a specific app, like a shared drive. For example, Slack or Salesforce. The limit is you must still check what data and actions the AI can reach. For a customer, it means less custom integration work.

prompt: A COO asks when a mid-market company is ready for agents. Explain the signs.

points.label: Four readiness signs
Gives a fitting workflow
Missing signs mean not ready
Land with ChatGPT Enterprise first

model: I look for four signs: a repeatable workflow with clear steps, data and systems the agent can safely reach, a business owner for the outcome, and a decision on what a human must approve. For example, order lookups and refunds in support. If those are missing, say messy data or no owner, they're not ready yet. For a customer like that, I'd land with ChatGPT Enterprise first and build toward agents.

prompt: A customer's agent keeps looping and costs are climbing. How would you design controls?

points.label: Hard limits on steps, spend and time
Gives a retry example
Limits cannot catch everything
Logs and alerts so people can step in

model: I'd put hard limits around the loop: a maximum number of steps, a spend cap and a time limit, so a runaway agent stops by itself. For example, an agent retrying a failing tool should give up and hand over to a person. Limits can't catch every edge case, so we also need evals on real tasks. For a customer, add logs and alerts, so their team sees what the agent did and can step in.

prompt: A security team asks whether their data will train OpenAI's models. How do you answer?

points.label: Not by default for business use
Names the products covered
Verify specifics; do not improvise
Send documentation, involve security early

model: For business products and the API, the position is that business data isn't used to train the models by default. For example, that covers ChatGPT Enterprise and API projects. I wouldn't go further from memory: retention, residency and certifications have specifics to verify, so I'd bring in a security specialist. For a customer, I'd send the standard security documentation and the trust portal early, and involve their security team from the start.

prompt: A customer asks the difference between data residency and inference residency. Explain.

points.label: Data residency is where data is stored
Inference residency is where the model runs
Shows they can differ
Availability varies by region
Diagnose, be precise, never promise a date

model: Data residency is where your data is stored at rest. Inference residency is where the model actually runs. They can differ: for example, content can be stored in Singapore while the model runs in another region. Availability varies by region, so check the current options. For a customer, I'd first ask whether it's a legal requirement or a policy, be precise about what's stored where, and never promise a date for something not yet supported.

prompt: A customer says "data must stay in Singapore". How do you handle the objection?

points.label: Diagnose before reacting
Shrinks the problem
If the law mandates, say so
Be precise and cite stronger controls

model: First I'd diagnose: is it a legal requirement, an internal policy, or general unease? I'd ask for the clause. Then I'd be precise about what's stored where, and about controls that often matter more, like no training by default, zero data retention and encryption. For example, we could land non-sensitive use cases first, or mask personal data before the call. If the law truly mandates in-country compute, I'd say so plainly and stay close.

prompt: A bank worries about staff pasting customer data into ChatGPT. What would you propose?

points.label: Layered prevention
Names controls
Never complete; residual risk remains
Separate API route with masking

model: Prevention is layered, never complete. Restrict staff to the company workspace, with SSO and admin settings, add data-loss-prevention tooling, and set a clear acceptable-use policy. For example, block personal accounts on company devices. Some risk always remains, especially free text, and that residual risk is their risk committee's call. For identifiable data, I'd propose a separate API route with masking, and onboard the vendor properly so a slip is a contained incident.

prompt: A customer asks how their support bot should behave when it does not know the answer.

points.label: Say it does not know and hand over
Gives the no-source case
Models can still give confident guesses
Test refusals in the golden set

model: A trustworthy bot says it doesn't know and hands over to a person, rather than guessing. For example, when retrieval finds no matching source for a policy question, it should decline and escalate with the context. The limit is that models can still give a confident guess, so you can't rely on instructions alone. For a customer, I'd put questions the bot should refuse into the golden set, test them, and track how often it hands over.

prompt: A CFO asks you to explain Snowflake's three layers and why the separation matters.

points.label: Storage, warehouses, cloud services
Storage and compute scale separately
Gives a team example
Oversized or always-on compute drives the bill
Pay for compute only while it runs

model: Snowflake has three layers. Storage holds the data as files in cloud storage, the shelves. Virtual warehouses are the compute, teams of workers that run queries. Cloud services is the manager with the access list and the index. Because storage and compute are separate, they scale independently. For example, finance gets its own warehouse without slowing operations. The risk is compute left running or oversized, which drives the bill. So customers pay for compute only while it runs.

prompt: A customer's analyst opens a dashboard. Walk me through what Snowflake does, end to end.

points.label: Permissions, then the optimiser plans it
Pruning and the result cache
Gives the dashboard example
Oversized or idle warehouses still cost
Cached results are free; auto-suspend stops billing

model: The BI tool sends SQL, for example orders by region this week. Cloud services checks the user's role and permissions, then the optimiser uses metadata to find which data chunks matter and skips the rest, called pruning. If nothing has changed, it can return a cached result with no compute. Otherwise a virtual warehouse reads only those chunks and returns the answer, then auto-suspends when idle. An oversized warehouse still racks up cost.

prompt: A customer asks how data gets into Snowflake and out to their tools. Explain.

points.label: In: ELT tools, Snowpipe, Kafka
Out: BI tools, apps and sharing
Names concrete tools
Data quality is still their job
Sharing means no stale extracts

model: Data comes in through ELT tools such as Fivetran, Snowpipe for continuous file loading, and Kafka for streams of events from operational systems. It goes out to BI tools like Tableau and Power BI, to apps, and to partners through data sharing, which gives them access to live data without copying it. The limit is that data quality is still the customer's job: duplicates and late feeds produce wrong dashboards. For a customer, sharing means no stale extracts.

prompt: A CFO asks how Snowflake's pricing compares with OpenAI's token pricing. Explain.

points.label: Both are consumption-priced
Compute time versus tokens
Gives a wasteful example
The signature is not the finish line
Watch usage with limits and dashboards

model: Both are consumption-priced: you pay for what runs. Snowflake bills compute time while a warehouse is running, and OpenAI's API bills tokens. For example, a warehouse left running or a bloated prompt both cost money without adding value. So the signature is not the finish line; the real number is usage months later. For a customer, that means watching usage with limits and dashboards, and right-sizing as workloads settle.

prompt: A customer wants an AI assistant over data in Snowflake. How would an LLM plug in? Walk me through it.

points.label: Snowflake stays the governed data layer
The app retrieves, then calls the model
Names the Cortex pieces
The model can still misread
Approved platform, model can be swapped

model: Snowflake stays the governed data layer, with its permissions, masking and row access policies. The AI app retrieves what the user is allowed to see, then calls the model with that context. For example, Cortex Search finds relevant documents and Cortex Analyst turns questions about tables into SQL. The model can still misread, so we add evals and citations. For a customer, the data stays in the platform they already approved, and the model can be swapped later.

prompt: A COO asks you to walk through how you would build a customer support assistant, end to end.

points.label: Sorts the message, then fetches the facts
A stronger model drafts; sensitive cases go to a person
Names what goes wrong, or why people stay involved
Says what to measure

model: A customer message arrives and a small, fast model classifies what they want. The system then fetches the right help articles and the order details through tool calls. A stronger model drafts the reply from those facts. Simple cases go out automatically, while sensitive ones go to a person with the draft ready. Wrong answers are the risk, so we start with heavy human review. We measure resolution rate, accuracy on a test set of real tickets, and satisfaction.

prompt: A finance director asks how AI would process supplier invoices, step by step. Explain the flow.

points.label: Reads the file and extracts fields in a fixed format
Checks it with rules; failures go to a person
Names what can go wrong
Writes to the finance system and measures it

model: First the system reads the invoice file and extracts the fields, such as supplier, date and total, into a fixed format using structured outputs. Next, plain rules validate the result: do the totals add up, is the supplier known, is it a duplicate. Anything that fails goes to a person as an exception. Clean ones are written into the finance system, often in an overnight batch. The risk is odd layouts and misread amounts, so we measure field accuracy.

prompt: A customer asks whether they need ChatGPT Enterprise or the API for their use case. How do you decide?

points.label: Enterprise is for staff using ChatGPT directly
The API is for building an app or automation
Gives a concrete use case
Asks who uses it and who builds; often both

model: I would ask who will use it and who will build it. If staff want help drafting, researching and analysing, ChatGPT Enterprise gives them seats with connectors and admin controls. If developers need to build the capability into their own app or automated workflow, the API is the fit. For example, a support team drafting replies suits Enterprise, while a customer-facing support bot suits the API. Many customers use both, landing with seats and expanding to the API.

prompt: A customer wants an internal HR and IT policy assistant. Connectors or custom RAG, and what goes wrong?

points.label: Starts with connectors or a Project, no build
Custom RAG for huge, spread-out or special needs
Names what goes wrong
Citations, owners and a real test set

model: I would start with connectors or a Project, because they link to SharePoint or Drive and respect each person's access without any build. Custom RAG makes sense for huge archives, many systems or special search needs. What goes wrong is usually permissions leaking restricted pages, outdated policies still being retrieved, and messy duplicate documents. So use citations, name an owner with review dates, and test on real staff questions.

prompt: A customer's pilot went well. How do you take the workflow from pilot to production?

points.label: Prototype, real-data evals, security, limited rollout
Picks by volume, risk and checkability; sets a baseline
Names the blockers
An owner, people on risky steps, then expand

model: Production is a path, not a switch. We pick a workflow with high volume, low risk and an easy way to check results, and record a baseline first. Then comes the prototype, evals on real data, security review, and a limited rollout with monitoring before scaling. Blockers are messy data, no owner and a security review started too late. A named business owner keeps people approving risky steps until evals earn trust, then we expand to the next team.
